a.title: Why Lean Startup is Betacode’s Rosetta Stone
a.lead: We started with an idea, a prototype and a lot of assumptions. Our first startup did not become a unicorn, but it taught us to build under uncertainty, kill bad ideas fast and listen to the market.
take: "People want this" and "people pay enough for this" are very different claims.
Build, measure, learn: the enemy of lean is certainty, not ambition.
Building got cheaper; building the wrong thing did not.

au.name: Pedro Gorrão
au.bio: Co-founder and CEO at Betacode. Writes about lean startup, building products and what we learn launching companies with our partners.

blocks.x: Wishmood was an on-demand delivery app for beaches, outdoor events and places traditional apps did not reach: food delivered to your sunbed, picnic or festival tent. The idea came from a real observation. Beachgoers wanted food, and nearby restaurants had no digital channel.
We built fast: app, restaurant onboarding, logistics and payments. But we learned that shipping is not the same as learning.

items: We assumed year-round demand, and it was strongly seasonal.
We built features before knowing whether restaurants could handle rush hours.
We optimised the app before proving the unit economics worked.
In interviews people loved the idea. Real usage told another story.

blocks.x: "People want this" and "people pay enough for this to be a business" are very different claims.

In 2016 we founded Betacode around a question: if lean methods helped us learn faster, could they help other companies do the same? Today it runs through everything we do: MVP development, technical consulting focused on what to build first, and Betacode Ventures, where we invest our team and let the market decide.

Eight years of domain knowledge and thousands of coaches. Instead of patching the old platform, we rebuilt it from scratch. In its first week it reached real users and validated its value proposition with paying customers.
What lean startup means in practice

items: Build: ship the smallest version that tests the riskiest assumption.
Measure: collect data from real users, not opinions from meetings.
Learn: decide whether to persevere, pivot or stop.

blocks.x: Startups: define the riskiest assumption before coding, almost always "will anyone pay?". Launch with one core workflow, not a feature matrix, and talk to users every week.
Tech companies: validate new product lines with prototypes before committing a team for six months, and measure outcomes (retention, revenue, support tickets), not output.
Traditional companies: start with the business problem, not a technology wish list. Pilot in one department and keep the old systems running while the new one proves itself.

items: Stealth build: six months in isolation and a launch nobody asked for.
Feature factory: shipping nonstop without checking whether usage or revenue moved.
Perfect architecture: months of infrastructure before any user touches the product.
Committee spec: 50 pages written by people who won’t use the software.
Sunk cost: carrying on because "we have already invested so much".

blocks.x: AI writes code faster and cloud infrastructure appears in minutes. The cost of building has dropped. The cost of building the wrong thing has not, and may have risen, because you can now ship bad ideas faster than ever.
What is the riskiest assumption? What is the smallest thing that tests it? What do the data say? Persevere or pivot? That is our Rosetta Stone.
